name: ChainHash
workload: SMHasher3 Speed test, bulk hashing of 262,144-byte inputs, bytes/cycle measured on the same binaries/host for chainhash, XXH3-64, rapidhash, komihash, UMASH-64 and CLhash.
claimed_speedup: 28.31 B/tick vs XXH3-64's 19.90 B/tick on Xeon 8375C (~1.4x); 26.26 vs 13.04 B/cycle on Apple M2 Pro (~2.0x) for 256KiB bulk inputs
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.5 on Linux 5.14 (Xeon, pinned to CPUs 16-23 with taskset); Apple Clang 17 on macOS (M2 Pro); SMHasher3 --test=Speed harness
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8375C; Apple M2 Pro
tradeoffs: Bulk-only design: short inputs (1-31 bytes) are much slower than XXH3-64 (155 Xeon ticks vs 29 per hash), so it is not a drop-in for small-key hash tables. Also ships a machine-checked (Lean) collision-bound proof and a ChainHash-128 variant; ChainHash-128 loses to XXH3-128 on Xeon (14.43 vs 19.82 B/tick) but wins on M2 Pro (14.43 vs 12.53 B/cycle).
caveats: Author (Thomas Ahle) also wrote and ran the benchmark; the repo's own reproduction pipeline (make speed, results/) mitigates but doesn't fully remove self-benchmarking bias. Released 2026-09-23, so no independent third-party confirmation yet.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs: thomasahle.com blog post 'Adversarial examples for fast hash functions' -> linked reproduction/benchmark repo -> thomasahle/chainhash

name: W1Hash
workload: Short-input hashing across a range of key sizes on an Intel Core Ultra 7 155H, comparing W1Hash against XXH3, wyhash and rapidhash.
claimed_speedup: Faster than wyhash (and its successor rapidhash) for inputs under ~16 bytes, per the README's benchmark chart; XXH3 remains fastest overall for most sizes
compiler_and_flags: clang, on Ubuntu (exact flags not stated)
tradeoffs: A wyhash variant tuned for short inputs; does not produce the same digests as wyhash, so it is not a drop-in replacement. Go port ships hand-written amd64 assembly plus a generic fallback; also embedded as a reference hash inside rurban/smhasher and fwojcik/smhasher3.
caveats: Benchmark is presented only as a PNG chart in the README, not as raw numbers or a linked benchmark script; exact compiler flags omitted; very new and low-visibility (4 stars).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs: gh search code 'w1hash' surfaced references in rurban/smhasher and fwojcik/smhasher3 pointing to canonical repo PeterRK/w1hash

name: falkhash2
workload: SMHasher3 bulk-hashing speed test (bytes/cycle), all registered hashes run on the same host/binary set; falkhash2 vs XXH3-64.
claimed_speedup: 18.43 bytes/cycle bulk vs XXH3-64's 12.82 bytes/cycle in the SMHasher3 results table (~1.4x, derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Requires the AES-NI aesenc instruction (AMD64-focused; performs poorly without it). Author explicitly warns it was found by trial-and-error against SMHasher and is 'likely heavily flawed' cryptanalytically; not intended as a general-purpose hash. The newer, stricter SMHasher3 now reports 6 failing tests.
caveats: The project's own README benchmark (2015) never names xxHash; it only claims to be faster than other SMHasher-passing hashes of that era on AMD/Intel CPUs (with GCC/clang/MSVC + CPU model stated). The direct xxHash comparison used here comes from the independent SMHasher3 results table (same run, same host), not from the project itself. Unmaintained since 2015.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs: gh search repos falkhash; cross-referenced against fwojcik/smhasher3 results/README.md speed leaderboard

name: CircleHash64f
workload: Hashing short inputs (4-256 bytes) with a 64-bit seed, comparing CircleHash64f against XXH3, XXH64 and SipHash on one machine.
claimed_speedup: 1.1x-1.8x faster than XXH3 across 4-256 byte inputs, e.g. 15.0 GB/s vs 8.19 GB/s at 256 bytes, 1.34 GB/s vs 1.21 GB/s at 4 bytes
tradeoffs: Go-only implementation (no C/C++ port located); CircleHash64fx variant trades some speed for a 128-bit seed and protection against multiply-by-zero state loss. Author explicitly says 'for best results, run your own benchmarks.'
caveats: No Benchmark-style test function found in the repo; the comparison table in the README is not backed by a runnable, published benchmark script, so methodology is only partially verifiable. Single machine, apparently single run.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs: gh search repos smhasher -> fxamacker/circlehash

name: MetroHash
workload: Bulk hashing and small-key hashing throughput compared against Google's CityHash 64-bit, 128-bit and 128-bit-CRC variants on an Intel Haswell machine.
claimed_speedup: Metro64: 50% faster than City64 bulk, 15% faster small keys. Metro128: 25% faster bulk, 60% faster small keys. Metro128crc: 30% faster bulk, 80% faster small keys.
hardware: Intel Haswell (exact model unspecified, author's 'typical' test environment)
tradeoffs: Optimized only for x86-64, explicitly no portability effort by design. Algorithmically generated hash family; statistical profile advertised as similar to MD5.
caveats: First-party blog claim only, no compiler or flags stated, CPU given only as 'Haswell'. Independent SMHasher3 testing (2025-2026) shows MetroHash variants failing 17-50 quality tests and posting lower absolute bulk throughput (4.9-6.0 bytes/cycle) than XXH3-64 (12.8 bytes/cycle) or rapidhash today, so the 2015 CityHash-beating claim is real but dated and CityHash itself is now a weak bar. Project unmaintained since 2022.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs: gh api repos/jandrewrogers/MetroHash/readme -> linked blog post jandrewrogers.com/2015/05/27/metrohash
